meta.descriptionEn: On 12 November 2014, a small robot called Philae dropped towards a comet and touched down on it. But it did not stay there. Its harpoons failed, its thruster never fired, and the lander bounced back up to about a kilometre above the surface before coming down again, twice. It ended up on its side in the shadow of a cliff. Yet it still sent back the first images from a comet's surface and the first on-site analysis of a comet's composition. Then it fell silent, woke up months later, and vanished again. This documentary follows the whole story: the ten-year journey, the failed anchors, the sixteen organic compounds, and the search for a lost lander.
meta.descriptionUr: 12 November 2014 ko ek chhota sa robot Philae ek comet par utra. Magar wo wahan tika nahi. Uske harpoons fail ho gaye, thruster chala hi nahi, aur lander uchhal kar takreeban ek kilometre oopar chala gaya. Aakhir wo ek cliff ke saaye mein, apne side par ja gira. Phir bhi us ne comet ki sateh ki pehli tasveeren aur pehla on-site analysis bheja. Phir wo khamosh ho gaya, mahino baad jaaga, aur dobara gum ho gaya. Is documentary mein poori kahani dekhiye: das saal ka safar, nakaam anchors, organic compounds aur khoye hue lander ki talash. Urdu aur English mein.

articleEn: On 12 November 2014, far from Earth, a small robot was descending toward the surface of a comet. Its name was Philae. Its first touchdown came at 15:34 UTC, but the most important thing that was supposed to happen did not happen: the harpoons never fired. As a result, the lander struck the surface and bounced back up. It rose at 38 cm/s and reached a height of about 1 km.

The danger was enormous. If that speed had risen to roughly 44 cm/s, the comet's gravity would not have been able to hold the lander. Meanwhile, at 16:03 UTC, a landing signal was received on Earth, but the scientists did not yet know that the lander had bounced. Later analysis showed that Philae had actually bounced twice, and that it finally came to rest somewhere other than the planned site.

So why did Philae bounce? Where did it finally stop? What did it discover? And could the lander ever wake up again? This article tells the whole story: how the plan came about, Rosetta's ten-year journey, and the day of the landing. Then we look at what Philae sent back from the surface, why its battery ran out, and what suddenly happened in June 2015.
This is not just a story of failure. It is a story in which history was made despite a mistake. So let's begin.

articleEn: The roots of this story go back to 1986. That year Halley's Comet came close, and several countries sent space probes toward it. The most prominent was ESA's Giotto. The probes sent back valuable information, but they also raised new questions. What was needed now was a mission that could study the comet's structure in more depth. So ESA and NASA began developing new probes together. NASA's project was CRAF, the Comet Rendezvous Asteroid Flyby. ESA's was CNSR, the Comet Nucleus Sample Return. Both missions were to use the same spacecraft design, called Mariner Mark II, to keep costs down.

Then came 1992. Because of budget constraints, NASA cancelled CRAF. ESA decided to build its own CRAF-like project. By 1993 it was clear that an ambitious sample-return mission was not possible within ESA's existing budget, so the mission was redesigned. The new plan was to first fly past an asteroid, then rendezvous with a comet, and carry a lander to land on it.

The mission was named Rosetta, after the Rosetta Stone, the slab on which a decree is written in three scripts. The lander was named Philae after an obelisk bearing inscriptions in both Greek and Egyptian hieroglyphs. Comparing the two helped in understanding hieroglyphs. The hope was that these two spacecraft would likewise open a window onto comets and the early Solar System.

Rosetta was first due to launch on 12 January 2003. The target was comet 46P/Wirtanen, which it would reach in 2011. Then, on 11 December 2002, an Ariane 5 ECA rocket failed during the launch of Hot Bird 7, and the rocket was grounded. Until the cause of the failure was known, a launch was not possible. In May 2003 a new plan was made: the target would now be comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The new launch date was set for 26 February 2004, with arrival at the comet in 2014.

However, this comet had more mass, and more mass meant a higher speed of impact on the surface. For this reason Philae's landing gear had to be strengthened. Finally, after two launch attempts were stopped, Rosetta lifted off on 2 March 2004 at 07:17 UTC from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana, aboard an Ariane 5 G+. The comet's two discoverers, Klim Churyumov and Svetlana Gerasimenko, were present at the spaceport at the time of launch. The total cost of the mission was about 1.3 billion euros.
But ten years still remained before the spacecraft would reach the comet. What happened along the way?

articleEn: Now Rosetta's journey begins. To gain the speed needed to reach comet 67P, it used gravity assist manoeuvres in the inner Solar System. The first Earth flyby took place on 4 March 2005. A few months later, on 4 July 2005, its onboard cameras watched comet Tempel 1 and the Deep Impact impactor collide.

Then came 25 February 2007, the day of the Mars flyby. The spacecraft was expected to pass just 250 km above the surface. The problem was that it would spend 15 minutes in the planet's shadow with no sunlight. The solar panels would be useless, and the spacecraft would have to run on batteries. It was placed in standby mode, and contact was not possible during that time. Because of this risk, the manoeuvre was called 'The Billion Euro Gamble'. The flyby succeeded. Rosetta also sent back detailed images of Mars's surface and atmosphere, and the mission continued according to plan. During this flyby, some of Philae's instruments were operated independently for the first time: CIVA took images, and ROMAP made measurements of Mars's magnetosphere.

The second Earth flyby took place on 13 November 2007. One astronomer mistook Rosetta for a small asteroid, and it was given the name 2007 VN84. On 5 September 2008 Rosetta passed asteroid 2867 Šteins at a distance of under 800 km, with a maximum relative speed between the two of 8.6 km/s. The third and final Earth flyby came on 12 November 2009. Then, on 10 July 2010, Rosetta passed asteroid 21 Lutetia at a distance of about 3,168 km.

On 8 June 2011 the spacecraft was put into spin stabilised mode. Everything except the onboard computer and the hibernation heaters was switched off. The hibernation was planned to last 31 months. Rosetta woke in January 2014, and in May 2014 it began a series of eight burns. These reduced the relative speed between the spacecraft and the comet from 775 m/s to 7.9 m/s, about 18 mph.

On 14 July 2014, images from the OSIRIS camera showed that comet 67P has an odd shape, with two distinct lobes. The larger lobe measures about 4.1 x 3.3 x 1.8 km, and the smaller about 2.6 x 2.3 x 1.8 km. The two are joined by a narrow neck. On 6 August 2014 Rosetta rendezvoused with the comet, and on 10 September it entered orbit around it at a distance of about 30 km.

Now a place had to be chosen for the lander. By 25 August 2014, five possible landing sites had been selected. On 15 September ESA announced Site J, on the smaller lobe. After a public contest it was named Agilkia. Did Philae get there?

Its basic structure was made of carbon fiber, including a plate, an instrument platform and a hexagonal sandwich. Its outer surface was covered with solar cells. Inside were ten instruments with a combined mass of 26.7 kg, a little more than a quarter of the lander's weight.

Among them, APXS measured elemental composition, CIVA's seven cameras took panoramic pictures, and ROLIS was a camera that took high-resolution images during descent. COSAC and Ptolemy analysed soil and gas samples. The SD2 drill could dig to 230 mm and had 26 platinum ovens. MUPUS measured the surface's density and mechanical properties, ROMAP studied the magnetic field, and SESAME probed sound and electrical properties in the layers beneath the surface. CONSERT had a different job: a radar signal from Rosetta passed through the comet to reach the lander, revealing the internal structure.

The biggest problem was gravity. On 67P, gravity is about 1/10,000 of Earth's, and the escape velocity is only about 1 m/s. One push, and the lander would be lost in space. So a multi-part landing plan was devised. The lander would separate from Rosetta at a 22.5 km orbit and descend on a ballistic trajectory, touching the surface at about 1 meter per second. The first part was the legs, which would absorb the initial shock so the lander would not bounce. The second was the ice screws, which would drive into the surface using the energy of the impact. Then a harpoon would fire at 70 m/s to anchor the lander. A thruster on top was meant to reduce the bounce at impact and also reduce the harpoon's recoil. On paper the plan looked complete.

Now the power. The lander had two batteries. One was a non-rechargeable primary battery of 1000 watt-hours, meant for the first 60 hours. The other was a secondary battery of 140 watt-hours, to be charged by solar panels. The panels had an area of 2.2 square metres and were designed to deliver up to 32 watts at 3 AU. Contact with Earth was to go through Rosetta, to use less power. The mission on the surface was planned for at least a week, and it was thought possible that it might last several months.

But the real test was still to come. On 11 and 12 November 2014, four go/no-go checks were carried out. Each check meant the team had to decide whether to permit the next step. Then, in the final tests before detachment, bad news arrived: the lander's cold-gas thruster was not working properly. It could not be fixed. Even so, the team gave a go. The lander would land with a faulty thruster.
Now a 100 kg machine was heading toward a comet where even a small mistake could be costly. Would the remaining systems be enough?

chapters.covers: 12 Nov 2014: detachment at 08:35 UTC, approach at about 1 m/s, first contact, reaction wheel switched off and the lander spinning every 13 seconds, striking a surface prominence, second touchdown at 17:25 and 3 cm/s rebound, final stop at 17:31 (S2 says 17:33), confusion in the science team, 28-minute signal delay. Why the harpoons failed (nitrocellulose, 0.3 g, unreliable in vacuum per the 2013 Copenhagen Suborbitals test).

articleEn: At 08:35 UTC on the morning of 12 November 2014, Philae separated from Rosetta, and the journey down began. The lander approached 67P at a relative speed of about 1 m/s, which is said to be equal to the comet's escape velocity. News took 28 minutes to reach Earth, so the control rooms were watching events with a half-hour delay.

At 15:34:04 UTC SCET, Philae touched the comet's surface for the first time. According to analysis, the initial impact was softer than expected. Telemetry showed that the harpoons had not deployed and the thruster had not fired. So neither of the systems meant to hold the lander to the surface worked. As a result, Philae bounced back at 38 cm/s and rose to a height of about 1 km. The escape speed was about 44 cm/s. The margin was small. If the speed had gone above 44 cm/s, Philae would have escaped the comet's gravity and never returned.

Philae had a flywheel, meant to keep the lander stable in orientation during descent. After touchdown it was supposed to shut down automatically. When touchdown occurred, the wheel's momentum was transferred back to the lander, and it began to rotate once every 13 seconds. During this first bounce, at 16:20 UTC SCET, the lander is thought to have hit a surface prominence. This reduced its rotation to one turn every 24 seconds.

When Earth's stations received the landing signal at 16:03 UTC, mission scientists did not know the lander had bounced. The lander had begun scientific measurements during this time. It was slowly moving away from the comet and then coming back down. Imagine data arriving and measurements being made, while the lander was not resting on the comet's surface at all. This is what confused the science team.

At 17:25:26 UTC SCET, Philae struck the surface a second time and rose slightly once more. The first bounce had been at 38 cm/s; the second was only 3 cm/s. The lander's speed had become very low. At 17:31:17 UTC SCET, the lander finally came to rest. The Rosetta source gives this time as 17:33 UTC, so the two sources differ slightly.

Later analysis showed that the lander had bounced twice, meaning there were three contacts with the comet's surface. The timeline was roughly this: first touchdown at 15:34, second at 17:25, and final stop at 17:31. In about two hours the whole story changed.

So why did the harpoons not fire? According to sources, the harpoon propulsion system contained only 0.3 grams of nitrocellulose. In 2013, Copenhagen Suborbitals showed that nitrocellulose is unreliable in a vacuum. This is one possible explanation. But the analysis only reported the outcome, that the harpoons did not fire. As to the real cause of the failure, this theory remains a guess.
So where had Philae stopped? Could work be done there? The next part is the story of that place, where light was very scarce.

articleEn: Philae's final location was in rough terrain, perhaps in the shadow of a cliff or crater wall. The lander was tilted at about 30 degrees. Light there was very limited: in each 12.4-hour comet day it got only 90 minutes of sunlight. ESA had expected the panels to fill the secondary battery. But the sunlight at this site, at least in this orbital phase of the comet, was not enough. So the first 60 hours of the primary battery were the real opportunity.

Philae was operated from the DLR Lander Control Center in Cologne, with CNES's SONC in Toulouse supporting it. By the morning of 14 November, the estimate of the battery charge was that only enough remained for the rest of that day. First, the instruments that needed no mechanical movement were run. These completed about 80 percent of the initial science observations. Then the command was given to deploy the MUPUS soil penetrator and the SD2 drill. After that, MUPUS data came back along with data from COSAC and Ptolemy. SD2 and MUPUS were important because they were to provide information from beneath the surface, but we will discuss their results in the next section. Finally, CONSERT's last data set was also downlinked.

Then, in the evening transmission session, an attempt was made. The lander was raised by 4 centimetres and its body rotated by 35 degrees, so that the largest solar panel could catch as much light as possible. But right after this, power began to fall quickly. All instruments had to shut down. The downlink rate kept dropping until it stopped. At 00:36 UTC on 15 November, contact with Philae was lost. The same day, Philae went into safe mode, or hibernation.

What was the reason? According to sources, the batteries ran out because the light was poor and the lander's orientation was not ideal. DLR's lander manager Stephan Ulamec said that before falling silent, the lander had sent all the science data of the First Science Sequence. He also said the machine had performed superbly in difficult conditions, and that the team could be proud of its incredible scientific success.

Philae sent images and data to Earth for about 64 hours, close to the 60 hours the primary battery was designed for. According to a source, had Philae landed at its planned site Agilkia, its mission would probably have ended by March 2015, because rising solar heating would have raised the temperature there.
Was there any hope from the shadowed spot? Mission controllers hoped that more sunlight would reboot the lander. But first, let's see what Philae found in those 64 hours.

The 2020 Nature report on primitive ice in boulders at the second touchdown site and the 25 cm drilling claim. Caveat: the sources differ on whether drilling worked, and on the deuterium result, since a 2024 re-analysis corrected the early 'three times Earth' finding.

articleEn: So what did Philae see in those 64 hours? Let's turn to the results from the instruments, which proved to be the mission's real treasure. First, the SESAME data. Scientists had expected the surface to be "soft and fluffy". But the first touchdown site turned out to be something else. According to SESAME, there was a layer of granular material about 25 cm deep, and beneath it a very large amount of water ice. The mechanical strength of this ice was also high, and cometary activity in the area was found to be low. In other words, there was something hard beneath the surface.

Now to the final landing site. Here the MUPUS instrument was to hammer into the ground. Power was gradually increased, but it could not go in far. The consistency of the site was described as like solid ice or pumice, meaning the surface was very hard. According to a source, this hardness may have been what obstructed the drilling. The SD2 drill completed all the steps to deliver a sample, but nothing entered the COSAC ovens. So the soil's elements could not be analysed.

However, COSAC detected molecules containing carbon and hydrogen in the comet's atmosphere, and this is where the organic story begins. At the first touchdown, COSAC measured material from beneath the lander that had been disturbed by the landing, while Ptolemy measured material from above the lander. The results of these two instruments revealed 16 organic compounds. Four of them had never before been seen on a comet. These four are acetamide, acetone, methyl isocyanate and propionaldehyde. The names are difficult, but the message is simple: comets contain complex organic chemistry.
What about amino acids? According to sources, only one amino acid has been found on a comet so far, glycine. Methylamine and ethylamine were found alongside it.

Another question: does comet 67P have its own magnetic field? According to measurements from ROMAP and Rosetta's RPC-MAG, the answer is no. Early on, Rosetta saw an oscillating magnetic field at 40 to 50 millihertz. But the results from Philae's landing indicate that it was probably due to the solar wind.

Now to 2020. On 28 October 2020, a report in the journal Nature said Philae had discovered low-strength primitive ice inside cometary boulders. This water ice was described as linked to the comet's formation about 4.5 billion years ago, and it was found mostly at the second touchdown site. According to the report, the lander made four separate surface contacts on two adjacent boulders there. In this way the bounce itself became an opportunity for science. The same report also said that Philae drilled 25 centimetres into the comet's boulder ice.
Here an important question arises, because another source says the lander could not drill and that nothing reached COSAC. There is a discrepancy between these two accounts, and we will not hide it.

Another disagreement concerns deuterium. According to one source, the ratio of deuterium to hydrogen in the comet's water was three times that of Earth's water. On this basis it was argued that it is hard for Earth's water to have come from such comets. But a new analysis in November 2024 caught a measurement error. After correction, the isotopic signature of 67P's water turned out to be Earth-like. So the possibility that Earth's water came from such comets remains acceptable.
So what was the result? Philae did only two days of science, but the results were very interesting. And then the story took a turn: Philae woke up.

chapters.covers: Wake-up on 13 June 2015 (85-second transmission, 24 W, −35 °C), contacts to 9 July 2015, CONSERT power-up, unstable links, no later contact, ESS switched off on 27 July 2016. Search using CONSERT and CNES-SONC (ellipse about 16 x 160 m), the OSIRIS candidate in April 2015, the confirmation on 2 Sept 2016 at 2.7 km showing the lander on its side in a crevice. Rosetta ended by landing in Ma'at on 30 Sept 2016. Legacy (first images from a comet surface, first in-situ analysis), lessons, open questions (O2 origin, oxygen, why it failed to anchor), CAESAR proposal passed over in 2019, and a request to like and subscribe.

articleEn: On 13 June 2015 at 20:28 UTC, ground controllers received an 85-second transmission from Philae, relayed by Rosetta. According to the message, the lander was in good condition. It had recharged its batteries enough to come out of safe mode. The lander reported that it was operating with 24 watts of power at −35 °C. So even in such cold, its systems were alive.

Then on 19 June 2015 there were two brief contacts, one at 13:37 UTC and another at 13:54 UTC. Each contact lasted about two minutes and brought status data. By 26 June, a total of seven intermittent contacts had taken place between the lander and the orbiter. The problem was that the link was not stable every time. On 5 July, a command was sent to power up the CONSERT radar. There was no immediate response. Then on 9 July the lander sent measurement data from that instrument. This was Philae's last communication.

Controllers could not give new instructions for investigations. As the comet grew more active, Rosetta had to be kept at a distance. By January 2016, controllers had accepted that further contact was not possible. On 27 July 2016, ESA switched off Rosetta's ESS.

But one question remained: where exactly was Philae? Its location was known to within a few tens of metres, but it could not be seen. Measurements from CONSERT placed the lander within an ellipse of about 16 x 160 metres. CNES-SONC narrowed this down further based on light and contact times. In April 2015, a deep analysis of OSIRIS-NAC data identified a candidate. In ESA's early communications it was called the "red candidate".

Then came 2 September 2016. As Rosetta descended to a distance of 2.7 km, the narrow-angle camera clearly saw Philae. Philae was wedged on its side in a dark crevice. That was why it got so little power. Now the context of its images became easy to understand. And on 30 September 2016, Rosetta ended its mission with a hard landing in the comet's Ma'at region.

What was the legacy? Philae took the first images from a comet's surface and carried out the first in-situ analysis. But some questions stayed open, such as where molecular oxygen, O2, came from. According to some researchers, O2 was incorporated when the comet formed. According to others, it could form on the surface when water molecules collide with silicates.

The lessons are also clear. The harpoons and thruster not working caused the bounce, and according to one source the nitrocellulose harpoon system had proved unreliable in a vacuum. Looking to the future, a proposed sample-return mission called CAESAR wanted to return to 67P. But in June 2019, NASA chose Dragonfly.
So was Philae a failure or a success? The decision is yours. If you liked the story, like the video and subscribe to the channel.

shorts.text: ایک ننھا robot ایک comet پر اترا، اور پھر دوبارہ خلا کی طرف اچھل گیا! 12 November 2014 کو Philae نے comet 67P کو پہلی بار چھوا۔ مگر اس کے harpoons fire ہی نہیں ہوئے، اور thruster بھی نہیں چلا۔ نتیجہ؟ lander 38 cm/s کی رفتار سے اوپر اچھلا اور تقریباً 1 km کی بلندی تک پہنچ گیا۔ اگر رفتار تقریباً 44 cm/s سے بڑھ جاتی، تو comet کی gravity اسے روک نہ پاتی۔ زمین پر 16:03 UTC پر landing کا signal پہنچا۔ سائنس دانوں کو اس وقت معلوم ہی نہیں تھا کہ lander اچھل چکا ہے۔ بعد میں پتا چلا کہ وہ دو بار اچھلا تھا۔ تو Philae آخر کہاں جا کر رکا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek nanha robot ek comet par utra, aur phir dobara khala ki taraf uchhal gaya! 12 November 2014 ko Philae ne comet 67P ko pehli bar chhua. Magar is ke harpoons fire hi nahin huay, aur thruster bhi nahin chala. Nateeja? lander 38 cm/s ki raftar se upar uchhla aur taqriban 1 km ki bulandi tak pohanch gaya. Agar raftar taqriban 44 cm/s se barh jati, to comet ki gravity ise rok na pati. Zameen par 16:03 UTC par landing ka signal pohancha. Science danon ko is waqt maloom hi nahin tha ke lander uchhal chuka hai. Baad mein pata chala ke woh do bar uchhla tha. To Philae akhir kahan ja kar ruka? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Philae touched down on comet 67P, but its harpoons and thruster failed. It bounced to about 1 km and no one on Earth knew at first.

shorts.titleEn: Rosetta's Billion Euro Gamble at Mars
shorts.text: ایک billion euro کا جوا، اور صرف 15 منٹ کا اندھیرا! 25 February 2007 کو spacecraft Rosetta کو Mars کے بہت قریب سے گزرنا تھا۔ اندازہ تھا کہ وہ سطح سے صرف 250 km اوپر ہوگا۔ مسئلہ یہ تھا کہ سیارے کے سائے میں 15 منٹ تک سورج کی روشنی نہیں ملنی تھی۔ Solar panels بیکار ہو جاتے۔ اس لیے spacecraft کو standby mode میں ڈال دیا گیا، اور اس دوران رابطہ بھی ممکن نہیں تھا۔ وہ ایسی batteries پر چل رہا تھا جو اس کام کے لیے بنی ہی نہیں تھیں۔ اسی خطرے کی وجہ سے اس manoeuvre کا نام پڑ گیا، The Billion Euro Gamble۔ تو کیا Rosetta بچ پایا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek billion euro ka jua, aur sirf 15 minute ka andhera! 25 February 2007 ko spacecraft Rosetta ko Mars ke bohat qareeb se guzarna tha. Andaza tha ke woh satah se sirf 250 km upar hoga. Masla yeh tha ke sayyare ke saaye mein 15 minute tak suraj ki roshni nahin milni thi. Solar panels bekaar ho jate. Is liye spacecraft ko standby mode mein daal diya gaya, aur is dauran rabta bhi mumkin nahin tha. Woh aisi batteries par chal raha tha jo is kaam ke liye bani hi nahin thin. Isi khatre ki wajah se is manoeuvre ka naam pad gaya, The Billion Euro Gamble. To kya Rosetta bach paya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In February 2007 Rosetta flew about 250 km above Mars and lost sunlight for 15 minutes. It ran on batteries not designed for the job, earning the nickname The Billion Euro Gamble.

shorts.roman: Mahinon ki khamoshi ke baad ek lander ne achanak paigham bheja! 13 June 2015 ko 20:28 UTC par ground controllers ko Philae ki taraf se 85 seconds ki transmission mili. Yeh signal Rosetta ne aage bheja tha. Paigham ke mutabiq lander bilkul theek halat mein tha, aur is ne batteries itni recharge kar li thin ke woh safe mode se bahar aa sake. Woh 24 watts power aur −35 °C par kaam kar raha tha. 26 June tak dono spacecraft ke darmiyan kul 7 intermittent contacts ho chuke thay. Magar link har bar mazboot nahin rehta tha. Phir 9 July 2015 ko aakhri rabta hua. Is ke baad Philae khamosh ho gaya. Kya yeh lander kabhi mil paye ga? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
